reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The .374 xwOBA and .507 xSLG sit in the 94th and 95th percentiles, yet his K% is 26.2 and his chase rate is high enough to keep the actual batting average well below what the quality-of-contact grades deserve. That's the whole tension in this profile: elite damage when he connects, genuine contact fragility when he doesn't. The projection resolves it optimistically, 44 home runs, a .924 OPS, and 39 stolen bases across 726 plate appearances, and the 11.5% walk rate suggests enough plate discipline to sustain the power rather than chase it into empty air. If the strikeout rate stays elevated and the chase doesn't come down, you're still looking at a power-speed outfielder with real run value; if it does come down, you're looking at a perennial MVP candidate.

reports.name: Jordan Walker
reports.published_report: The contact-and-chase tension is what makes Walker hard to pin down: 92.5 mph average exit velocity and a 12.8% barrel rate that would look at home on a middle-of-the-order bat, paired with a 35.9% chase rate that sits near the bottom of the league. The raw power translates — .468 xSLG says the thump is genuine, and 29.1 ft/s speed turns singles into doubles and steals into a real weapon. But he's giving pitchers a road map: expand the zone, watch him swing, collect the strikeout, and that 25.4% K rate is the tax he's currently paying on every plate appearance. If he ever sharpens the strike-zone recognition to match the contact quality, the .279/.335/.483 projection starts to look conservative; if he doesn't, he's a 30-homer, 20-steal corner outfielder who leaves runs on the table every time a pitcher decides to pitch around the zone.

If the contact quality holds and the discipline stays roughly where it is, he's a legitimate dual-threat shortstop hitting in the middle of a lineup; if the chase rate worsens against pitchers who figure him out, he trends toward a volatile, strikeout-heavy version of that same player.

reports.name: Michael Harris II
reports.published_report: The .287 xBA sits at the 95th percentile and the xSLG comes in at .474 — what that says is that when he makes contact, he hits it hard and where it needs to go, and the projection's .290 AVG with 27 home runs is the natural extension of that shape. The problem is the other end: a 44.5% chase rate and 3.7% walk rate, both at the 2nd percentile, mean his floor is entirely dependent on pitchers failing to expand the zone against him. If a staff starts attacking consistently, the contact quality gets buried under volume, and you're left with a good average and real power thinned out by an ugly OBP. He's a second-division regular if the discipline stays broken, a borderline star if the barrel stays in fair territory.

reports.name: Walker Jenkins
reports.published_report: The contact rate is the headline: 15% strikeouts across AAA & A+ & A translates to 18.7% at the MLB level, well below where most big-league hitters land, and that's with a .237 ISO in tow. At 21, Walker Jenkins is posting a .417 OBP across those three levels while walking 43 times against only 50 strikeouts in 324 plate appearances, a combination that scouts get excited about precisely because disciplined hitters with real power don't usually need much fixing. The ISO translates to .171 at the MLB equivalent, above what most regulars produce, so the power isn't a minor-league mirage, but his ceiling as an everyday center fielder depends on how much of that contact quality survives a full diet of big-league velocity. If it doesn't hold, you're looking at a useful bench piece; if it does, the Twins have a true regular.

reports.name: Ronald Acuña Jr.
reports.published_report: The .362 xwOBA tells you the talent is still there; the 29.5% whiff rate tells you the knee isn't fully back. That gap between elite expected slugging (.481 xSLG) and a middling exit velocity picture is what post-ACL Acuña looks like right now: the barrel rate is legitimate at 12.3%, the 11.5% walk rate shows the eye held, but the bat is getting beaten more often than before the injury. reports.name: Zach Neto
reports.published_report: The gap between an 11.6% barrel rate and a 30.6% strikeout rate is the whole profile: Neto makes genuine, hard contact when he connects, but he chases at a 37.8% clip and whiffs at 32.7%, which keeps his xBA down at .213 and drags xwOBA to .310. The power is calibrated honestly by the projection, 28 home runs over 703 plate appearances, because the barrel rate earns that, but the batting average ceiling is capped by the contact issues and .319 OBP reflects that ceiling rather than hiding it. Add 22 projected steals and you have a shortstop who produces counting stats at an above-average rate through volume and athleticism, not through any advantage in the batter's box. If the chase rate ever moves toward league norms, this looks like a legitimate middle-of-the-order piece; if it doesn't, he's a low-.240 hitter posting 25-plus home runs whose offensive value lives and dies by the run environment around him.

reports.name: Luis García Jr.
reports.published_report: The contact and power metrics are legitimate, the walk rate is a real problem. García's xBA sits at .286 (94th percentile) and his xSLG at .507 (95th percentile), which is what you'd expect from a hitter with a 12.7% barrel rate and 91.7 mph average exit velocity: the batted-ball quality is genuine and consistent. But a 4.5% walk rate puts him near the bottom of the league, and a 38.6% chase rate explains exactly why: pitchers can expand the zone and skip the risk of working into his wheelhouse. The projection calls for a .288/.320/.547 line with 32 home runs, and that holds if his swing decisions stay roughly where they are; if pitchers learn to exploit the chase more aggressively, the .320 OBP starts looking generous and everything downstream gets smaller.

reports.name: Tyler Bremner
reports.published_report: The K-BB% across AA & A+ sits at 24%, and the translation puts that at 14.9% in an MLB context, a tick above league average, which is roughly what you'd expect from a back-end starter who misses bats without embarrassing himself in the walk column. A 12.4 K/9 against 3.3 BB/9 across 72.6 innings is the kind of combination that grades well against his peers, but the ERA sitting at 4.3 with a 1.3 WHIP suggests the stuff plays cleaner in counting terms than in results. If the strikeout rate translates and the control holds, he's a fifth starter who earns regular turns; if the walks tick up at the next level, the bullpen is the honest floor and the back-end ceiling shrinks with them.

reports.name: Jac Caglianone
reports.published_report: The contact quality is almost absurdly good for a 23-year-old, and the discipline is the reason this doesn't add up to more. A 93.1 mph average exit velocity and 54.4% hard-hit rate sit in rarified company, and an xSLG of .502 explains why 25 home runs project even with a .819 OPS that undersells the raw thump. But a 39.3% chase rate and 5.8% walk rate mean pitchers have a reliable escape hatch, and until that closes, the Statcast ceiling and the actual production line will keep living in different zip codes. If the plate discipline tightens even modestly, he profiles as a middle-of-the-order force; if it doesn't, he's a power-first corner bat who requires careful roster construction around the strikeout and walk numbers.

reports.name: Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
reports.published_report: The Statcast contact picture here is genuinely strange, in a way that demands an explanation rather than a celebration. His xBA sits at .285, a 93rd-percentile contact quality mark, yet his xSLG is .405, right at the median, and a 6.8% barrel rate that ranks in the 42nd percentile is the reason: he's hitting the ball well enough to avoid outs at an elite clip but not doing enough damage when he does. The projection's .267/.338/.375 slash reflects that imbalance, 11 home runs across 627 PA is the output when a hitter makes near-elite contact without the loft or authority to convert it into extra bases at a commensurate rate. The whole profile hinges on whether he rediscovers the lift that made him a genuine power threat, because if contact quality this good never translates into a better barrel rate, you're left with an above-average on-base presence at a corner position, which is a useful player and not quite enough.

His 31.4% whiff rate and 35.3% chase rate are genuinely elite-tier stuff metrics, and the underlying contact quality, a 3.72 xERA against contact that's running right at league average exit velocity, says the swing-and-miss is doing real work, not masking a crooked barrel rate. The problem is the 10.0% barrel rate, which undercuts everything and explains why the projection lands at a 4.73 ERA over 113.2 innings despite the strikeout profile. The whole outcome hinges on whether he limits squared-up contact more consistently, because if he does, the 27.1% strikeout rate and 7.0% walk rate make him a mid-rotation piece worth protecting on a LAD depth chart that can afford to wait.

reports.name: Matt Olson
reports.published_report: The xSLG sits at .509 and the barrel rate at 14.7%, and neither number needs an asterisk — 92.8 mph average exit velocity with a 51.8% hard-hit rate is a contact quality profile that belongs near the top of the league. The tension is entirely between that raw power and a 24.9% strikeout rate that suppresses the batting average, leaving the xBA at .248 while the xwOBA climbs to .355. If the strikeouts stay where they are, the projection's .250/.325/.506 slash is the ceiling of what the hit tool can do, not a floor. Forty-two home runs across 703 projected plate appearances is what you get when the contact quality is elite and the contact rate is merely tolerable, and that profile points to a near-certain 40-homer first baseman with a middling average for as long as his legs let him stay in the box.

reports.name: Brayan Rocchio
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is almost entirely a bottom-of-the-card story, except for one thing that matters: he strikes out only 14.6% of the time. That contact rate keeps him on the field and keeps the counting stats alive, but a 3.1% barrel rate and 86.9 mph average exit velocity mean the contact itself is rarely doing damage. His projected .246/.306/.375 line across 596 plate appearances puts his OPS at .681, a second-division regular's number, not an everyday shortstop's. What makes this profile work at all is the fielding, a 98th-percentile OAA mark that says he earns his roster spot with his glove, and 20 projected steals add a little texture to a bat that otherwise lives near the bottom of a lineup. If the contact quality doesn't tick up as he settles into his mid-twenties, he's a defensive specialist with speed, and that's a fine big-league career, just not the one Cleveland probably envisioned when they built around him.

reports.name: Christian Zazueta
reports.published_report: The command-and-control profile here is almost absurdly clean for a 21-year-old at this level. Zazueta has walked 20 batters across 103.7 innings at AA & A+, a 1.7 BB/9 that translates to a 2.4 MLB equivalent, well below the league-average 3.2. The strikeout rate holds up too, with 144 punchouts producing a 30% K-BB% that would sit comfortably clear of the 13.5% MLB-average translation. Everything hinges on whether the stuff plays against better bats, because a back-end starter ceiling isn't a criticism, it's the outcome if the profile holds, and a multi-inning relief role is what's left if it doesn't carry past AAA.

reports.name: Travis Bazzana
reports.published_report: The walk rate tells you what Bazzana actually is right now: 11.5% BB%, a genuine skill, paired with a 25.7% chase rate that ranks comfortably below the league median. The problem is everything that happens when he does make contact. An xBA of .231 and a 4.8% barrel rate put his contact quality in the bottom fifth of the league, and the projection (.249/.343/.394) reflects exactly that tension — a patient hitter whose bat-to-ball and raw power aren't yet carrying the profile. If the discipline holds and the contact quality climbs even modestly, 21 projected stolen bases and a solid OBP floor give him a path to a useful everyday second baseman; if the xSLG of .353 is where he actually lives, he becomes a high-walk, low-damage type who needs the speed to stay relevant.

reports.name: Angel Martínez
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the problem, and it might be the whole profile. At 3.1%, essentially the floor of the league, Martínez has almost no margin for error when pitchers locate, and his 41.9% chase rate explains exactly why they keep trying. The contact quality sits in a strange middle place: his xBA reads .257 and his whiff rate is a tidy 20.0%, so he puts the bat on the ball often enough, but the 87.6 mph average exit velocity and 35.7% hard-hit rate say the contact isn't doing much damage. The projection's .731 OPS across 406 PA reflects all of that, solid-ish bat-to-ball, real speed with 12 projected steals, some pop at 16 home runs, but a .287 OBP that points toward a second-division regular ceiling and a bench seat if the chase rate stays where it is.

If he can't, the 21 projected home runs come wrapped in a .684 OPS and the conversation shifts to bench utility rather than everyday center.

reports.name: Javier Sanoja
reports.published_report: An 8.0% strikeout rate is genuinely rare at the big-league level, and that's the whole argument for Sanoja — the bat-to-ball is extraordinary, but the power profile that surrounds it is not. His xSLG sits at .350 and his barrel rate at 2.1%, which means he's making elite contact with the ball and then doing very little to it; the .289/.330/.439 projection line assumes he squeezes more value out of that contact than the Statcast shape currently suggests. If the exit velocity at 87.0 mph and 31.7% hard-hit rate represent his true ceiling, this is a high-average, low-walk gap hitter who tops out as a second-division regular, and the OPS projection of .769 may be optimistic. The profile holds if the contact quality creeps up even modestly as he ages into his mid-twenties; if it doesn't, that strikeout rate buys him a long career as a useful, limited bat rather than anything more.

reports.name: Justin Crawford
reports.published_report: The sprint speed is elite, the bat isn't. Crawford runs at 29.5 ft/s, 96th percentile, but an xwOBA of .286 and a 1.5% barrel rate paint a contact-over-power profile with almost no margin for error in the box. He makes enough contact that the 17.4% K rate plays well, but a 38.0% chase rate and 6.0% walk rate mean he's living dangerously against pitchers who can locate, and the projection's .315 OBP shows exactly how little cushion there is. If the speed translates into 18 stolen bases and he holds that chase rate rather than letting it climb, Crawford is a useful bottom-of-the-order everyday piece; if pitchers crack the zone-expansion problem, what's left is a pinch runner in an outfielder's body.

reports.name: Braxton Ashcraft
reports.published_report: That 37.0% chase rate is doing real work here. Ashcraft gets hitters to expand at a clip that ranks among the most extreme in the league, and the 5.2% walk rate shows he's not buying it with free passes. The strikeout number sits at 25.9%, respectable but not overwhelming, which means the profile hinges on whether he can keep manufacturing soft contact when hitters don't chase. Hard-hit rate at 41.6% and average exit velo at 89.7 mph is where this gets interesting: those two are pulling in opposite directions, and the xERA of 3.42 suggests the contact management is holding well enough that the projection's 3.65 ERA and 166.3 innings feels like a reasonable landing spot for a mid-rotation starter who misses fewer bats than you'd expect from a guy throwing 97.3 mph.

Across A+ & A this season, he's running a 10% strikeout rate against a 15% walk rate in 292 plate appearances, and those translate to a 16.8% K rate and 10.6% walk rate at the MLB level, both better than a league where the average hitter punches out 22% of the time. The power is where the ceiling closes: a .120 ISO across A+ & A that translates to .105, well shy of the MLB average of .150, and the 19 stolen bases are the compensating tool that keeps the profile from reading as one-dimensional. If the bat-to-ball gift and speed hold as he climbs, he's either a bench bat or a platoon piece at the top; if the power never comes, the bench is the ceiling, not the floor.

reports.name: Elmer Rodríguez
reports.published_report: The 2.50 ERA at AAA looks like a front-line starter's line until you look under it. His 102 strikeouts across 101.7 innings translate to an 8.2 K/9 equivalent in the majors, a tick below where MLB starters average, and the 49 walks translate to a 4.1 BB/9 when the MLB average sits at 3.2. That gap is the whole tension: the ERA says ace, the walk rate says something closer to a relief profile, and the K-BB% translation of 11.1% confirms there isn't enough separation to carry a rotation spot if the command doesn't sharpen. If it doesn't hold, what's left is a multi-inning arm or setup piece, which is a real role, just not the one the ERA advertises.

reports.name: Cristofer Torin
reports.published_report: The contact grades out at the 99th percentile among AA hitters this season, and 62 strikeouts across 556 plate appearances is a real skill, not a small-sample quirk. Cristofer Torin hits .281 with an 11% strikeout rate at AA at 21, and the MLB-equivalent translation puts his K% at 15.3 against a league that whiffs at 22.0% — that gap is the whole argument for him. The problem is everything else: his translated ISO sits at .129 while the MLB average runs at .150, and his walk rate translates to 7.5% where the average sits at 8.5%, so the ceiling math just doesn't add up to a regular. If the power develops toward his current .160 ISO in a harsher run environment, you have a legitimate everyday shortstop candidate; if it stays where the translation says it lives, you have a very good bench bat with a contact profile that plays.

reports.name: Alex Bregman
reports.published_report: The contact profile is stubbornly ordinary: 88.2 mph average exit velocity, a 5.8% barrel rate, a 37.2% hard-hit rate that trails most regulars. What carries Bregman is discipline, a 15.8% whiff rate and 23.5% chase rate that both sit well clear of league average, pairing with a 10.8% walk rate to prop up an OBP the raw power numbers alone couldn't support. The projection calls for 27 home runs across 722 plate appearances, which is a lot to ask from a profile that doesn't barrel the ball at a premium rate; it gets there if the power translates more cleanly to Wrigley than the exit velocity suggests it should. He's a solid everyday third baseman as long as the discipline holds, but if the power doesn't play up, you're left with a high-OBP regular whose ceiling and floor start to look uncomfortably similar.

reports.name: Seaver King
reports.published_report: The .308 average across AAA & AA is the loudest thing in this profile, and the BABIP behind it is the problem. A .367 BABIP is doing a lot of carrying, and the MLB-equivalent translation shows the ISO deflating to .160, barely a tick above league average, once you run it through the level discount. At 23, King has shown 15 steals and a 10% walk rate across 489 plate appearances, so the profile isn't empty, but the K rate translates to 23.3% in MLB context, nearly indistinguishable from what an average big-leaguer runs, and the ceiling here is already labeled organizational depth. If the BABIP normalizes and the power doesn't play up, what's left is a bench piece with some speed and a passable eye, not an everyday shortstop.

reports.name: Zyhir Hope
reports.published_report: The .513 slugging and 29 home runs at AA at 21 are loud, but the profile's tension lives in the translation gap. That ISO of .226 against his peers in the AA hitter pool reads as legitimate pop, yet when you run it through an MLB lens it softens to .166, which clears the MLB average of .150 but not by the margin the raw line suggests. The strikeout rate is the hinge: 25% at AA translates to 27% against MLB arms, and a right-field profile with that much swing-and-miss needs the power to stay loud when the pitching gets smarter. If it does, and the 26 stolen bases suggest there's more to the game than just the bat, Hope can grow into a regular; if the contact rate erodes further, you're looking at a bench piece who hits for power in spurts.

reports.name: Justin Wrobleski

reports.name: Kazuma Okamoto
reports.published_report: Thirty-four projected home runs with a 13.7% barrel rate is the argument for Okamoto, and the counterargument lives one row away: a 33.1% whiff rate that craters his xBA to .224. The power is genuine in shape, a 90.6 mph average exit velocity with barrels at the 90th percentile, but all that contact quality gets eroded by strikeouts at 29.3%, leaving a .236 projection and a profile that flatters slugging while punishing average. He's a lineup piece you roster for the 34 homers and the .462 SLG, not the batting line surrounding them, which means his value is entirely contingent on whether Toronto puts him somewhere the thump matters more than the strikeouts. If a pitcher finds his whiff zone consistently, the power still shows up in clusters, just with enough outs around it to keep him from being more than a middle-of-the-order bat with a real flaw.

He's either a useful table-setter if the bat-to-ball skill translates, or a bench piece with a pretty minor-league line.

reports.name: Spencer Torkelson
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is a case study in one number undermining everything else. Torkelson's 22.1% chase rate ranks in the 91st percentile, genuine elite contact management, and his 11.9% barrel rate is legitimately above average. But a 31.5% whiff rate in the strike zone means pitchers don't need to expand; they're beating him with pitches he's supposed to hit, which is how a hitter with real barrel talent ends up with a .212 xBA in the 6th percentile. The projection reads like the sum of that contradiction: 25 home runs over a full 606 PA, a .314 OBP that reflects the walk rate, and a .222 average that reflects everything else. He's a second-division regular as long as the zone whiff rate stays where it is, and a genuine middle-of-the-order piece if he ever solves it.

reports.name: Joey Cantillo
reports.published_report: The 29.6% whiff rate is the one number that flatters him, and the 12.0% walk rate is the one that keeps undoing it. Cantillo misses bats at a rate that fits a real rotation piece, but his chase rate sits at just 27.7%, meaning hitters are generating those whiffs mostly on pitches in the zone rather than expanding off it, which is a fragile recipe when his command slips. The 4.17 xERA and .314 xwOBA reflect that tension honestly: the stuff plays well enough to steal strikes, but not well enough to survive the free passes, and a 92.2 mph fastball at the 17th percentile leaves almost no margin for error when he falls behind. If the walk rate compresses, he's a back-end starter who earns the 3.9 ERA the projection gives him across 159.8 innings; if it doesn't, he's a reliever hiding in a rotation spot.

reports.name: Nathan Church
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is almost entirely a warning label. His 85.7 mph average exit velocity and 30.0% hard-hit rate sit at the bottom of the league, and a .289 xwOBA says the bat isn't hiding anything. What keeps him from being a simple non-tender is the contact discipline: a 17.2% strikeout rate is genuinely good, and 28.5 ft/s sprint speed gives him a base-running dimension most soft-contact profiles can't claim. The problem is a 42.1% chase rate that undermines every bit of that, turning the walk rate into a near-irrelevant 5.6% and leaving him with no margin for error if pitchers stay off the plate. The projection's .676 OPS across 458 PA is the honest ceiling given the contact quality, and if the chase rate doesn't come down, he's a bench piece who runs well and puts the ball in play — not a regular.

reports.name: Gary Gill Hill
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole argument. Across AAA, AA, and A+ this season, Gary Gill Hill has issued just 29 walks in 139.7 innings, a 1.9 BB/9 that translates to a 2.4 MLB-equivalent BB/9, and that control profile lands in the 98th percentile among pitchers with 20-plus innings in 2026. The catch is the strikeout side: 119 punchouts across those same levels sounds fine until the translation puts the MLB-equivalent K/9 at 6.8, a full two ticks short of the 8.6 league average, and a 14th-percentile mark in the current pool. If the stuff can play up in shorter stints, he becomes a multi-inning or setup reliever whose command is a genuine weapon; if the whiff rate doesn't climb, the floor is a depth arm who walks nobody but also doesn't miss enough bats to hold a roster spot.

reports.name: Robert Gasser
reports.published_report: The exit-velocity numbers are genuinely interesting and genuinely confusing at the same time. Hitters are making contact at 86.5 mph average exit velocity against Gasser, a reading that ranks in the 92nd percentile, yet his Hard-Hit rate sits at 33.3%, which is among the worst you'll find at this level. That split, soft contact in aggregate but frequent hard contact when they do barrel him up, points to a guy who gets a lot of weak rollers and popups but has almost nothing to offer when a hitter squares one up, which tracks with a 22.4% Whiff rate and 28.6% Chase rate both sitting near the 30th percentile. He commands the zone well enough, a 7.2% walk rate puts him in the 71st percentile there, but the strikeout rate at 22.1% is roughly league average and there's no swing-and-miss weapon in the profile to make the walk prevention pay off. The projection of a 4.28 ERA over 107.5 innings is a fine back-end outcome if the weak-contact shape holds, but if big-league hitters figure out the timing and stop rolling over, the whiff rate offers no safety net.

reports.name: Aron Estrada

But the translation undercuts the power story pretty hard — that ISO compresses to .153 in MLB context, right at league average, because Double-A juice doesn't travel. The walk rate is the sharper problem: 6.3% translated, against a league baseline of 8.5%, and the raw 82nd-percentile contact rate won't compensate if pitchers learn to let him chase at the next level. If the bat-to-ball skills hold and the power plays even close to average, he's a low-end regular at second; if the walk rate stays where it is and the power deflates, what's left is a bench bat with a ceiling question.

Fifty stolen bases in 554 plate appearances tell you the speed is genuine and probably propping that batting average up, and the contact rate is real enough — 108 strikeouts against 61 walks translates to a K% just a tick above league average at the MLB level, with walk rate that clears the bar. The ceiling here is a bench bat who steals bases and gets on base at a passable clip; the floor is a fringe roster piece whose hit tool looks more like a function of legs than bat.

reports.name: Roki Sasaki
reports.published_report: The whiff rate and the walk rate are pointing in opposite directions, and that's the whole Sasaki puzzle right now. His 29.7% whiff rate and 33.4% chase rate say the stuff genuinely misses bats, but a 9.4% walk rate is bleeding those gains dry, and the contact quality when hitters do connect is ugly: 43.1% hard-hit rate, 10.0% barrel rate, an xERA sitting at 4.43. The 97.8 mph fastball is the engine, and if he learns to command it rather than just throw it, the strikeout rate climbs and the walk rate drops enough to make the rest of this forgivable. If the command doesn't come, 129.3 innings of a mid-rotation ERA profile with a bloated WHIP is what a Dodgers club expecting more gets.

reports.name: Dante Nori
reports.published_report: The calling card is a 16% strikeout rate that translates to roughly 20% at the MLB level, and 17 stolen bases across AA & A+ & A say there's a real athlete underneath the profile. The problem is everything else: a .238 average with a .282 BABIP and a translated ISO of .108, well short of the MLB mean of .150, mean the bat isn't carrying its weight, and the walk rate barely clears 9% while still coming in under its MLB equivalent of 8.1%. If the contact quality doesn't climb as he settles into a full AA diet, the speed and strikeout discipline are orphaned tools with nowhere to attach. The floor here is bench depth, and without a meaningful jump in his ability to do damage when he connects, that's probably where the ceiling lands too.

reports.name: Jake Munroe
reports.published_report: The profile is built almost entirely on contact and patience, and the power is where the case gets complicated. Across AA & A+, Munroe is hitting .289/.402/.498 with 63 walks against 90 strikeouts in 516 plate appearances — a 17% strikeout rate that translates to roughly league-average contact frequency at the big-league level, and a walk rate that comes out above the MLB mean. The ISO of .209 across those levels is the loudest number, but the MLB-equivalent translation cools it to .150, exactly at league average, which means the ceiling hinges entirely on whether the raw pop holds any shape against upper-level pitching. If it does, he's an everyday third baseman; if the power flattens and the translation is right, a well-disciplined bench bat is what's left.

reports.name: Will Sanders

If the command tightens, he's a depth arm; if it doesn't, he's still a depth arm, just one who doesn't stick.

reports.name: Evan Carter
reports.published_report: The chase rate is the loud number: 20.6% puts him in elite company for plate discipline, but the bat-to-ball underneath it is a problem. A 29.2% whiff rate against that low a chase rate means he's not chasing, he's just missing what he does swing at, and the .199 xBA is the result. The walks (10.8 BB%) keep him from being a roster afterthought, and 28.9 ft/s gives him a real stolen-base path, which is why the projection carries 17 steals even against a .197 average. If the contact ever catches up to the eye, you have a useful everyday outfielder; if it doesn't, he's a speed-and-walks bench piece who runs the bases well and not much else.

reports.name: AJ Blubaugh
reports.published_report: The 28.7% whiff rate is doing real work here, but the walk rate is quietly eating the profile alive. reports.name: Harry Ford
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole profile. Ford has drawn 45 walks against 65 strikeouts across 257 AAA plate appearances in 2026, and that 18% walk rate translates to 12.8% at the MLB level — genuine plate discipline at a position where patience alone buys roster value. The problem is everything else: a .223 average, four home runs, and an ISO of .112 at AAA that translates to .116 at the MLB level, well short of what catchers typically need to hold a lineup spot. If the eye stays and contact ticks up enough to leverage those walks into real OBP, he's a backup catcher with an unusually patient approach worth keeping; if the bat stalls where it is, the walks sustain a career without earning him a regular role.

reports.name: Bryant Betancourt
reports.published_report: The contact is the calling card. Across AAA & AA in 2026, Betancourt has struck out in just 14% of his 406 plate appearances, and the MLB translation puts that at 17.9%, well below what most big-league hitters produce. The .218 ISO across that same sample says the power is already at a usable level for a catcher, translating to .162 at the MLB level, above the 22.0% strikeout environment he'd be operating in. The .335 OBP is where the ceiling starts to close: the walk rate hasn't kept pace with the contact quality, and if that gap doesn't narrow, what you have is a bat that makes a lot of quiet contact without doing enough damage to profile as more than a bench piece, either a plus defensive backup who gives you league-average offense at a premium position, or a fringe roster name if the glove doesn't carry its weight.

reports.name: Devin Taylor
reports.published_report: The .416 BABIP is doing real work here, and that's where the argument lives. Across AAA & AA & A+, Taylor is hitting .312/.414/.494 with 93 walks and 168 strikeouts in 628 plate appearances — the contact and patience numbers look elite against the hitter pool, but the MLB-equivalent translation bleeds the shine off: that 27% strikeout rate translates to 29.2% against big-league pitching, and the ISO that reads as above-average in the minors translates to just .138, well short of where power-first outfielders need to land. The walk rate carries over reasonably well at 11.6%, so the floor is a patient outfielder who reaches base, but if the BABIP regresses and the strikeouts stay where they translate, there isn't enough power to keep a team from eventually running him out of the lineup. Either a low-end regular with a favorable park and contact luck, or a bench left-handed bat who gets by on walks.

reports.name: Willson Contreras
reports.published_report: The .375 xwOBA tells you almost everything: elite contact quality, real power, an 11.1% walk rate that keeps the on-base number honest. What makes it odd is the profile underneath, a 30.7% whiff rate and 34.3% chase rate that both sit near the bottom of the league, which means the damage comes despite genuine swing-and-miss issues, driven almost entirely by a 13.3% barrel rate that keeps the exit velo looking ordinary while the power production stays extreme. If pitchers find a way to bury him consistently in his chase zones, the strikeouts climb and the .383 OBP projection softens; the whole thing hinges on whether he keeps barreling enough to offset the contact vulnerability. At 34, behind the plate in Boston, the projection of 28 home runs and an .895 OPS says frontline offensive catcher, and the Statcast profile, gaps and all, backs that up.

Suarez is a depth arm if it stays together, and a depth arm if something slips.

Across A+ & A in 466 plate appearances, Neyens has walked 114 times against 155 strikeouts, a 24% walk rate that sits at the 99th percentile of his hitter pool, paired with a 33% strikeout rate that lands at the 10th. The .429 OBP is genuine because he earns first base constantly, but that on-base engine is running alongside a BABIP of .351, and if contact quality doesn't improve the average falls further from the already-modest .231. The translated profile is the honest reckoning: the walk rate stays elite at 16.1%, but the strikeout rate translates to 37.1% while the ISO, which looks respectable on the farm, comes out below the MLB mean at the big-league level, so the ceiling here is either a disciplined bench piece who finds a platoon niche or, more likely, organizational depth.

reports.published_report: Forty-two stolen bases across AA & A+ is the loudest thing on this card, and the plate discipline behind it, 74 walks against 107 strikeouts in 522 PA, is what makes the speed sustainable rather than reckless. His translated walk rate of 11.2% clears the MLB average of 8.5% by a meaningful margin, suggesting a hitter who can get on base without leaning on contact, which is exactly the profile you want underneath that kind of baserunning aggression. The power doesn't travel: his .134 ISO across AA & A+ translates to .113 at the MLB level, well short of the .150 MLB average, and that gap is the whole tension in the profile. If the speed holds and the OBP replicates, you have a usable everyday center fielder; if the ISO stays buried and the strikeout rate ticks toward its translated 23.4%, what's left is a bench piece who steals bases when he gets on.

reports.name: Blake Mitchell
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the loudest thing on this card, and it's also the problem. At A+ in 2026, Blake Mitchell has drawn 113 walks in 511 plate appearances, a 22% clip that sits at the 99th percentile of his pool, and he's added 27 stolen bases and 23 home runs on top of it, a legitimately unusual combination for a catcher at 21. But the .234 average against a .346 BABIP tells you the strikeouts aren't disappearing, and when that contact rate translates to an MLB-equivalent 36.8% K%, what survives the jump is a 15.4% walk rate propped up against average power at .152 ISO. The whole profile hinges on whether the discipline holds as pitchers locate better, because if the strikeouts climb and the walks compress even modestly, the .234 average becomes the story rather than the footnote. If it works, he's a patient, borderline-average offensive catcher who runs; if it doesn't, the bench is the ceiling.

reports.name: Matt McLain
reports.published_report: The tension in McLain's profile is the gap between his 26.4% chase rate, genuinely good plate discipline backed by 10.3% walks, and a 27.3% strikeout rate that buries him anyway. When he does make contact, the barrel rate sits at 9.4%, but 88.3 mph average exit velocity and 36.4% hard-hit rate say most of those barrels are the exception, not the shape of his contact. The .191 projected AVG with a .284 OBP is the profile in miniature: he earns walks, whiffs too much, and doesn't hit the ball hard enough often enough to rescue the batting average when the strikeouts land. If the strikeout rate cools even a little and the speed (84th percentile) keeps working on the bases, the 19 projected steals and 17 home runs make him a useful, if thin, second-division regular; if it doesn't, a .630 OPS second baseman is a roster problem.

reports.name: Brent Headrick
reports.published_report: A 2.04 ERA projection with a 3.00 xERA underneath it leaves less room for skepticism than you might expect. Headrick's 30.0% strikeout rate and 32.0% whiff rate are the engine: he misses bats at a clip that holds up even when sequencing regresses, and a 4.7% barrel rate means the contact he does allow is mostly soft. The walk rate sits at 7.8%, which is the one lever that could pull this apart — if the zone command slips, there isn't a dominant fastball (94.2 mph) to bail him out, and the profile shifts from high-leverage asset to matchup piece in a hurry. As a 30-hold arm projecting 79.5 innings, he profiles as a genuine late-inning option for New York, and the Statcast numbers suggest that's a role he can sustain rather than one he's outrunning.

reports.name: Carlos Gutierrez
reports.published_report: Thirty-one stolen bases at A+ from a left-handed bat hitting .271/.380/.431 in 415 plate appearances is a louder profile than the ceiling suggests. The discipline translates well enough: 59 walks against 80 strikeouts at A+ becomes 10.6% walks and 23.4% strikeouts at the MLB level, both directionally fine, with the walk rate sitting above the MLB mean. The power doesn't make the same trip, with an MLB-equivalent ISO of .122 where the typical big leaguer sits closer to .150. If the speed holds and the hit tool keeps the OBP functional, he's a useful bench piece with a real late-inning role; if the bat flattens against upper-minors velocity, the speed alone doesn't carry a corner outfielder's profile.

reports.name: Jose Chirinos
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the best part of this profile, and the strikeout rate is the problem. Across A+ & A, Chirinos has posted a 3.3 BB/9 and a 3.4 ERA over 114 innings, which grades well inside his pitcher pool, but his 9.9 K/9 translates to roughly 7.5 at the MLB level, a tick below what MLB starters typically need to stick. A 17% K-BB% sounds workable until the translation cuts it to 11.0%, well short of the 13.5% MLB average. The floor and ceiling land in the same place: a depth arm whose viability depends entirely on whether the strikeout rate grows as the competition does, and if it doesn't, the command advantage alone won't hold a big-league job.

reports.name: Angel Feliz
reports.published_report: Thirty-six stolen bases at A+ is the loudest thing in this profile, and it's carrying a lot of weight. Everything else in the line is quiet: .232/.308/.370 across 495 plate appearances, and the MLB-equivalent translation has his strikeout rate at 27.2%, well above where it needs to be to stick, with almost no power translating out, ISO coming out at .110. The speed is genuine, but if he can't make enough contact to get on base at a usable clip, the legs become a minor asset rather than a carrying tool. Bench depth is the realistic ceiling here, and only if the hit tool takes a step forward.

reports.published_report: The sample covers 298 PA in Triple-A, Double-A, High-A, and Single-A, so confidence is high; the damage plays in games. The miss rate keeps that power from showing up consistently. The contact points to a reserve today, but the damage leaves an everyday path open.

reports.name: Brooks Auger
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the argument: 85 punchouts across 59.7 innings at A+, and the K/9 translates to 9.1 at the MLB level. But the walk rate is holding this profile together with tape. At A+, 4.8 BB/9 translates to 4.6 at the MLB equivalent, while the MLB average sits at 3.2, and that gap is wide enough to swallow the strikeout advantage almost entirely, his MLB-equivalent K-BB% landing at 13.2% where the league average is 13.5%. The profile hinges on whether the command tightens as he climbs, because if it doesn't, the swing-and-miss just pays rent on the walks instead of building anything, and the ceiling here is a depth arm either way.
reports.report: The bat-missing is starter-caliber; the stuff is ahead of the strike throwing right now. Keep the starter path open, but the walk rate has to move before the bullpen risk fades. The sample covers 59.7 IP in High-A, so confidence is low.

reports.name: Ryan Sprock
reports.published_report: The contact and plate discipline are genuinely loud for a 21-year-old catcher at this level: a 13% strikeout rate across A+ & A that translates to roughly 18.9% in an MLB context, and 70 walks against just 57 strikeouts in 427 plate appearances. The .422 OBP is the profile's best argument, and the walk rate translating to 11.6% MLB-equivalent gives it teeth — most big-league regulars don't sniff that figure. The power is the ceiling question: a .121 ISO equivalent at the major-league level is thin, and if that gap doesn't close as he climbs, what's left is a bat-control specialist who catches, which is a bench piece, not a regular. Either an everyday backstop who figures out how to generate more damage, or a very patient backup who makes quiet contact behind the plate.
reports.report: The open question is damage. He consistently finishes at-bats with contact. Everyday contact regular; high-contact bench floor. The sample covers 427 PA in High-A and Single-A, so confidence is low.
